extracted.intended_audience: media professionals, journalists, media researchers and readers interested in news production and press influence
extracted.subtask_description: A snapshot methodology for classifying online news stories as 'original' or 'non-original' based on evidence of journalistic endeavour and the source of the story (press release, social media, wire, rival publisher, etc.). Used to compare output across major UK commercial news websites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadly speaking we counted content as original if it appeared to involve some journalistic endeavour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reporter was merely repeating facts assembled elsewhere (on TV, Instagram, Twitter etc.) we’ve counted it as non-original content. The Mirror and Manchester Evening News content from the same Reach network was counted as original because it was 'uncovered by reporters at the same publisher.' For agency copy, it was counted as original if it looks like it was produced exclusively for that title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-original content (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Content judged to be non-original consists of pieces where reporters merely repeat facts assembled elsewhere or where there is little evidence of journalistic endeavour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples flagged as non-original include articles based on social media posts (Instagram, TikTok), TV shows, widely distributed newswire copy (AP, PA), picture galleries, SEO rewrites of easy-to-obtain information, and promotional/e-commerce pieces with affiliate links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency copy originality rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency or wire copy is treated differently depending on exclusivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency copy was counted as original if it 'looks like it was produced exclusively for that title.' By contrast, AP and PA copy — because it is widely used across the media — was counted as non-original in the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intra-publisher (network) content rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Content shared across titles within the same publisher/network may be counted as original under certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study counted Mirror and Manchester Evening News items that also appeared elsewhere in the Reach network as original because they were 'uncovered by reporters at the same publisher.' (The authors note that discounting such intra-network pick-ups would lower The Mirror's original-content tally.)

rubrics_metrics.name: SEO stories criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: SEO-driven pieces are judged for originality based on how much journalistic endeavour they exhibit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study counted SEO stories as non-original when they are 'basic rewrites of easy-to-obtain information which appear to involve little journalistic endeavour.' The Sun in the sample had SEO stories counted as non-original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional/e-commerce with affiliate links
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotional articles tied to e-commerce or containing affiliate links are classified as non-original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Sun had six stories in the snapshot that were promotions for e-commerce containing links to affiliate advertisers; these were treated as non-original content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media / broadcast-sourced stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories whose primary source is social media platforms or broadcast TV are treated as likely non-original unless additional journalistic work is evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study specifically flagged Instagram, TikTok and various TV shows as major sources of non-original stories for some publishers (e.g., Instagram was the biggest source for The Sun). If a reporter simply repeats or republishes material from those platforms, it is classed non-original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture galleries classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Picture galleries are regarded as a form of non-original content for the purposes of this snapshot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In The Guardian sample three of the judged non-original items were picture galleries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-classification taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: The study classifies the origin of stories into discrete source types to determine originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source categories used include: press releases/public announcements, social media (Instagram, TikTok), TV shows, newswires (PA, AP and other agencies), other publishers/rival titles, promotions/e-commerce/affiliate content, SEO-driven pieces, picture galleries, and intra-network republishing. Counts per category are reported per publisher in the snapshot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling methodology and caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis is a time-limited snapshot with methodological caveats that affect interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors examined the first 100 stories published by the UK’s then-six most popular commercial news websites on the morning of Tuesday 21 June (a few hours' output). They note the research 'is just a snapshot' and involves 'some fairly arbitrary judgments about what counts as original journalism.' They caution that sampling one morning may miss publishers' original journalism that appears at other times of day and that readers should view the full spreadsheet and create their own judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold: 'enough journalistic endeavour' test
rubrics_metrics.description: A qualitative threshold used to decide originality: whether an article contains 'enough journalistic endeavour' to pass the originality test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an intentionally subjective standard applied across the sample (e.g., 'We judged that 16 out of 100 articles published on the morning of 21 June 2022 [in The Guardian] did not contain enough journalistic endeavour to pass the originality test'). The page emphasises that some calls were arbitrary and open to challenge.
